When one tree is attacked by insects, some forests can smell the alarm on the wind and prepare their own defences. Old trees feed young ones through these underground lines, which researchers have nicknamed the "wood wide web". Experiments suggest that a mother tree can recognise her own saplings and favour them slightly. None of this is magic; it is chemistry, carried slowly. But it changes how a forest feels: a walk among trees passes over conversations that have been running for centuries. Foresters now speak of keeping old trees alive as "mother trees" for the young. In a forest, losing touch with the network is as dangerous as losing the light. Trees, it turns out, are social before they are timber. Forests that are cut into pieces lose these connections first, which is why small woods grow sick even when the trees look green. Saving a forest, researchers now say, means saving the ground beneath it.

lessons.chinese: 章鱼有九个"脑"、三颗心和蓝色的血液，它也许是我们这颗星球上最接近"外星智慧"的生命。在实验室里，章鱼会开罐子、记路线、认出具体的饲养员，还会朝讨厌的灯喷水。德国一家水族馆的章鱼学会了瞄准灯泡喷水来关掉那盏烦人的灯——一次又一次，直到短路永远解决了问题。这一切了不起的地方在于，章鱼的身体构造与我们毫无相似：它的神经元散布在八条腕足里，每条腕足都能尝味、触探并自行决定。事实证明，智慧并不需要一副人类的形貌。这也给厨房与实验室提出了一个安静的伦理问题：面对一只会回望我们的动物，我们该如何对待它？一些国家已把章鱼列入受保护的研究动物名录。好奇，是有后果的——对我们，也对它们。
lessons.english: An octopus has nine brains, three hearts and blue blood, and it may be the closest thing our planet has to an intelligent alien. In laboratories, octopuses open jars, remember routes, recognise individual keepers, and spray water at lights they dislike. One octopus in a German aquarium learned to switch off an annoying lamp by aiming water at the bulb — again and again, until a short circuit solved the problem for good. What makes this remarkable is that an octopus is built nothing like us: its neurons are spread through its eight arms, and each arm can taste, touch and decide on its own. Intelligence, it turns out, does not require a human shape. This raises a quiet ethical question for kitchens and laboratories alike: how should we treat an animal that watches us back? Some countries have added octopuses to their lists of protected research animals. Curiosity has consequences — for us, and for them.

lessons.chinese: 珊瑚礁覆盖的海底不到百分之一，但约四分之一的海洋生物会在那里度过生命的一段时光。当水温过高，珊瑚虫会排出住在体内、给自己颜色和养分的微小植物；礁体随之变白，这一现象称为"白化"。白化的珊瑚并没有死，但它在挨饿，反复的热浪不给它恢复的时间。潜水员形容健康的珊瑚礁是喧闹的城市——枪虾在脆响、猎食鱼在游弋、海龟在清洁站排队；而白化的礁体是无声的废墟。希望并非出于多愁善感，而是有科学依据：较冷水域的珊瑚礁在近年的热浪中存活得更好，这说明在人类改变习惯的同时，保护当地环境可以为它们争取时间。珊瑚长得极慢，长一米要花一个人的一生。一个世纪建成的，几个炎热的夏天就能拆掉。大海记着账，只是不急于出示。
lessons.english: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the sea floor, yet about a quarter of all sea life spends part of its life there. When the water grows too warm, coral animals drive out the tiny plants that live inside them and give them both colour and food; the reef turns white, an event called bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving, and repeated heatwaves leave no time to recover. Divers describe healthy reefs as noisy cities — snapping shrimp, hunting fish, turtles waiting at cleaning stations — and bleached reefs as silent ruins. The hope is not sentiment but science: reefs in cooler waters survived recent heatwaves better, which suggests that protecting local conditions buys time while the world changes its habits. Reefs grow slowly — a human lifetime for a few metres. What a century built, a few hot summers can undo. The sea keeps the score, and it is in no hurry to show it.

lessons.chinese: 冰川是一段用冰写成的漫长记忆。数百年前落下的雪被压成一层层，每一层都保存着那一年的记录：火山灰、花粉、古代矿井的铅，还有凝固成气泡的、人们呼吸过的空气。科学家向下钻探，把过去当书页翻阅。冰川也记录人类的错误：在汽车出现之前很久，工业烟尘就已染黑了阿尔卑斯的冰层。如今，这份记忆正在融化。世界各地的冰川都在退缩，而它们退去时，释放出曾被冷藏的东西——滋养河流的水，也有在低温中等待多年的细菌与物质。山下的社区正在适应：有人每年在岩石上标记冰线，像在给病中的父母量身高。一座冰川消失，损失是双重的——滋养山谷的水，和那座告诉我们"过去的空气是什么样子"的档案馆。原来，冰是我们最古老的图书馆，而它正在被一排排拆掉。
lessons.english: A glacier is a long memory made of ice. Snow that fell centuries ago is pressed into layers, and each layer keeps a record of its year: volcanic ash, pollen, lead from ancient mines, and bubbles of the very air people once breathed. Scientists drill down and read the past like pages. Glaciers also record human mistakes: industrial soot darkened the ice of the Alps long before cars existed. Now the memory is melting. Glaciers worldwide are retreating, and as they go they release what was stored — water for rivers, but also bacteria and materials that waited in the cold. Communities below are adapting: some mark the ice line on the rocks each year, the way you measure a sick parent. When a glacier disappears, the loss is doubled — the water that fed the valley, and the archive that told us what the air used to be. Ice, it turns out, was our oldest library, and it is being taken down, shelf by shelf.

lessons.chinese: 人类工程师已经开始像学徒拜师那样研究动物。白蚁建造自带空调的塔楼：尽管外面是热带酷暑，巢穴内部的温度几乎恒定，奥秘在于一座会呼吸的迷宫隧道。津巴布韦一座著名的办公楼复制了这个原理，只用普通塔楼十分之一的能源就保持了凉爽。黄蜂咀嚼木头造"纸"；蜜蜂设计的六边形蜂巢不浪费一丝空间——这种几何结构，人类靠计算才证明是最优解。就连完全由活体组成的蚁桥，也会根据"交通量"自动调整宽度。这些生物没有一个学过力学。它们的蓝图写在本能里，并在一亿年的试错中被反复打磨。建筑师们把这种方法称为仿生——学的是设计，而非装饰。昆虫建筑师给人的教训令人谦卑：最好的工程之所以看起来毫不费力，是因为进化早已替它付清了全部代价。
lessons.english: Human engineers have begun studying animals the way apprentices study masters. Termites build towers with built-in air conditioning: despite tropical heat outside, the temperature inside their mounds stays nearly constant, managed by a labyrinth of tunnels that breathe. Engineers copied the principle in a famous office building in Zimbabwe, which stays cool with one tenth of the energy of ordinary towers. Wasps build paper by chewing wood; bees design six-sided cells that waste no space, a geometry humans only proved optimal by calculation. Even an ant bridge, made entirely of living bodies, adjusts its width to the traffic. None of these creatures studied mechanics. Their blueprints are written in instinct and refined by a hundred million years of trial. Architects now call this approach biomimicry — learning the design, not the decoration. The lesson of the insect builders is humbling: the best engineering often looks effortless because evolution has already paid for it, in full, over ages.

lessons.chinese: 鸟窝看起来像一堆垃圾，除非你亲手搭一个试试。织布鸟用喙打出上百个结，把湿草编成一只挂在枝头、风干后紧实如篮的绿巢。缝叶莺用从蛛网上抽来的丝线把叶子缝在一起——在真正的叶子上，缝出真正的针脚。雨燕用羽毛和唾液胶成的巢贵重到引发收藏者与保护者之争。就连那些"懒惰"的鸟也很聪明：有些猫头鹰直接搬进老鹰的旧巢，把力气留给蛋。每一个巢都是安全、保暖与伪装之间的折中，并为某一个确切地点的危险量身调试。当然，杜鹃干脆省掉全部工程，把蛋下在别人的巢里。研究鸟巢的科学家不断发现其中的工程学：减震、控温、排水。换句话说，巢不是一个仅凭本能搭起的家，它是对一长串问题的小小解答——而且是在没有双手的情况下完成的。
lessons.english: A bird's nest looks like a pile of rubbish until you try to build one. A weaver bird ties hundreds of knots with its beak, weaving wet grass that will dry into a tight, green basket hanging from a branch. A tailorbird sews leaves together using threads pulled from spider webs — real stitches, in real leaves. Swifts glue feathers and saliva into nests so valued that they cause arguments between collectors and conservationists. Even the "lazy" birds are clever: some owls simply move into an old hawk's nest, saving their strength for the eggs. Every nest is a compromise between safety, warmth and camouflage, tuned to the dangers of one exact place. Cuckoos, of course, skip the work altogether and lay their eggs in the nests of others. Scientists studying nests keep discovering engineering: shock absorption, temperature control, and drainage. A nest, in other words, is not a home built from instinct alone; it is a small solution to a long list of problems — solved without hands.

lessons.chinese: 北极光的开场，奇怪地，在太阳上。太阳表面的风暴抛出带电粒子流；一两天后，粒子流抵达地球，我们行星的磁场充当盾牌，把大部分粒子弯折向两极。在那里，远在天气之上，粒子撞击稀薄的空气，令其发光——氧发出绿色，氮发出红色与紫色。地面上听不到任何声音；这场演出完全静音，而且免费。如今科学家能提前一天预报强极光，"极光游客"飞往北方，站在严寒里。北方的古老民族另有解释——是灵魂在嬉戏，或动物的亡魂——他们以敬畏而非好奇对待极光。物理学家也会同意：极光值得敬畏。它们是一个可见的提醒——地球每天都被一层看不见的磁盾守护着；没有它，我们的大气层会被同一股"画天空的风"慢慢剥走。
lessons.english: The northern lights begin, strangely, on the sun. Storms on the solar surface throw out streams of charged particles; a day or two later the stream reaches earth, where our planet's magnetic field acts as a shield, bending most particles towards the poles. There, high above the weather, they strike the thin air and make it glow — green for oxygen, red and purple for nitrogen. No sound reaches the ground; the show is completely silent, and free. Scientists can now predict strong displays a day ahead, and "aurora tourists" fly north to stand in the cold. The old peoples of the north had different explanations — spirits playing, or the souls of animals — and treated the lights with respect rather than curiosity. Physicists would agree the lights deserve respect: they are a visible reminder that the earth is defended every day by an invisible magnetic shield, without which our atmosphere would slowly be stripped away by the same wind that paints the sky.

lessons.chinese: 沙漠并非空无一物；它是一张"解决方案清单"。水也许一年只落一次，于是沙漠生命用发明作答。骆驼的驼峰储存的是脂肪而非水，它可以失去体重的四分之一而无恙——这样的失重对多数动物是致命的。有些青蛙用泥茧把自己封在地下，等待数年后的那场雨。耳廓狐昼伏夜出，排泄中几乎不损失水分。植物也加入了答卷：沙漠玫瑰用落叶停止"出汗"，有些花的种子能在地下等待几十年，只为一场好雨——然后几周之内发芽、结籽、消失。连时间安排都是设计好的：许多沙漠花只在凉爽的夜里开放。沙漠里没有任何东西被浪费。它是地球上最严酷的设计学校，而它的毕业生——那些留存下来的动植物——是大多数人类从未修习过的这门学科的大师：如何靠几乎一无所有活下去。
lessons.english: A desert is not empty; it is a list of solutions. Water falls perhaps once a year, so desert life has answered with inventions. The camel stores fat, not water, in its hump, and can lose a quarter of its body weight without harm — a loss that would kill most animals. Some frogs seal themselves underground in a kind of mud cocoon and wait years for rain. The fennec fox hunts at night and loses almost no water in its waste. Plants join in: the desert rose sheds its leaves to stop sweating, and the seeds of some flowers can wait decades underground for a single good storm, blooming in weeks, setting seed, and vanishing. Even the timing is engineered: many desert flowers open only at night, when the air is cool. Nothing in a desert wastes anything. It is the strictest school of design on earth, and its graduates — the plants and animals that remain — are masters of a subject most of us have never studied: how to live on almost nothing.

lessons.chinese: 河流会改变主意。几个世纪里，大河的下游能在平原上像一根松开的水管一样摆动，身后留下一幅它历次"决定"的地图：牛轭状的湖泊，以及土壤中古河道的痕迹。黄河历史上曾摆动数百公里，淹没整片整片的郡县——这就是为什么中国史书提到它时，总带着敬意与恐惧。河流一搬家，一切都跟着搬：鱼群、商路、边界和村庄。现代工程师用堤坝与堤岸把河流"钉住"，但河流有的是耐心。泥沙在不受欢迎的地方悄悄聚集，为旧日的自由而进行的争夺仍在继续。地理学家如今在造桥之前会研究"古河道"，因为河流记得自己所有的旧河床。这对任何做长期规划的人都是一课：自然同意我们的计划，只是暂时的。河流没有迷路。它只是在田野之下等待轮到自己。
lessons.english: Rivers change their minds. Over centuries, the lower course of a great river can swing across a plain like a loose hose, leaving behind a map of its old decisions: curved lakes called oxbows, marks of old channels in the soil. The Yellow River historically wandered by hundreds of kilometres, drowning whole districts, which is why Chinese historians speak of it with respect and fear. When a river moves, everything moves with it: fish, trade routes, borders and villages. Modern engineers try to pin rivers down with dams and banks, but rivers are patient. Sediment gathers where it is not wanted, and the battle for the old freedom continues quietly. Geographers now study "historic channels" before building bridges, because a river remembers its old beds. There is a lesson in this for anyone who plans anything long-term: nature agrees to our plans only for a while. The river is not lost. It is only waiting, under the fields, for its turn.

lessons.chinese: 种子是寄给未来的信，而植物发明了各种寄信的妙法。有些种子长着钩子，靠皮毛旅行——你袜子上粘的苍耳就是这么来的。有些给自己造了丝绸降落伞，乘着风跨过整条山谷；一株兰花可以带上一百万颗。红树把"活的幼苗"直接放进潮水，椰子则横渡大洋，漂上几个月，在陌生的海岸生根。有些种子非要先经历冒险才肯发芽：某些松果只在火中打开；许多沙漠种子要被砂砾磨伤外皮才会苏醒。科学家曾唤醒收藏了几百年的种子。一粒种子携带着植物的全部计划——一条根、一根茎、两片子叶，还有一份打包好的午餐——只为等待三个信号：水、温暖和光。植物无法逃离坏年成。于是它们学会了另一种办法：派孩子们去旅行。有的种子走一米，有的走一片海洋。无论哪种，母株都看不到终点——所以种子必须携带一切：计划、午餐，还有运气。
lessons.english: A seed is a message sent to the future, and plants have invented remarkable ways to post it. Some attach hooks and travel by fur — that is the origin of the sticky burrs on your socks. Others build parachutes of silk and cross whole valleys on the wind; a single orchid may carry a million of them. Mangroves drop live young into the tide, and coconuts cross oceans, floating for months before taking root on a stranger shore. Some seeds demand adventure before they will grow: certain pine cones open only in fire, and many desert seeds germinate only after being scarred by sand. Scientists have revived seeds from collections centuries old. A seed carries a plant's whole plan — a root, a stem, two leaves, and a packed lunch — waiting for three signals: water, warmth and light. Plants cannot run from a bad year. So they learned, instead, to send their children travelling. Some seeds travel a metre; some travel an ocean. In both cases, the parent never sees the destination — which is why a seed must contain everything: the plan, the lunch and the luck.

lessons.chinese: 我们在不同的年纪重读同一本书，遇见的是不同的书。十五岁读《简·爱》，读到的是爱情；三十五岁读，读到的是贫穷与自尊的研究；五十岁再读，也许读到的是对愤怒的沉思。文字没有变，变的是读者：我们把自己活过的每一年都带到第一页上，而那本无法改变的书，映照出我们。这就是为什么老师们恳求学生别卖旧书。一排翻旧了的经典，是过去的你用一种你仍然读得懂的语言写成的日记。重读也带来原谅：二十岁时显得乏味的段落，到了四十岁，往往恰好承载着你那时的重量。伟大的书之所以伟大，不在于它艰深，而在于它被写得足够宽阔，装得下不止一种人生。经典不会老。我们会——重读，就是测量这种衰老的方式。
lessons.english: We reread the same books at different ages and meet different books. At fifteen, "Jane Eyre" is a love story; at thirty-five, it is a study of poverty and pride; at fifty, perhaps, a meditation on anger. The words have not changed. What has changed is the reader: each of us brings every year we have lived to the first page, and the book, which cannot change, reflects us. This is why teachers beg students not to sell their old books. A shelf of well-worn classics is a diary written by your former selves, in a language you can still read. Rereading also forgives: passages that seemed dull at twenty often carry exactly the weight of one's forties. Great books are not great because they are difficult; they are great because they were written wide enough to hold more than one life. The classics do not age. We do — and rereading is how we measure it.

lessons.chinese: 笔记本电脑赢得了与纸的大多数战役，但有一个领域纸仍在获胜：手写笔记。对比研究显示，手写——因为慢，所以必须取舍——比全部敲录带来更深的理解。键盘邀请你逐字抄录；笔逼迫你做决定。手写还为大脑自己的速记留出空间：箭头、圈点、页边的涂鸦，把一个想法画出来，而不是写一串关于它的句子。许多科学家和写作者坚持纸笔笔记正是为此：纸页不仅记下想法，还记下想法周围的气氛——而那件事后来被证明很重要。纸还有别的长处：它不会没电，不会"叮"地弹出通知，公式旁的一幅草图在任何一次软件升级中都不会消失。这并不是要封杀电脑——论存储与检索，电脑胜过任何书架。更聪明的习惯是让工具匹配任务：屏幕负责存储与分享，纸负责思考。最慢的记笔记方式，可能仍是最快的理解方式。
lessons.english: Laptops have won most battles with paper, but in one field paper keeps winning: note-taking by hand. Research comparing students finds that writing by hand — slowly, and therefore selectively — produces deeper learning than typing everything. A keyboard invites transcription; a pen forces decision. Handwriting also leaves room for the mind's own shorthand: arrows, circles, sketches in the margin, drawings of an idea rather than sentences about it. Many scientists and writers keep paper notebooks for exactly this reason: the page records not just the idea but the mood around the idea, which turns out to matter. Paper has other virtues: it never runs out of power, it cannot ping, and a drawing next to a formula survives every software update. None of this bans laptops, which store and search better than any shelf. The wiser habit is to match the tool to the task: screens for storage and sharing; paper for thinking. The slowest way to take notes may still be the fastest way to understand.

lessons.chinese: 守时常被当作一种小小的美德，一个礼貌问题。其实它是一种"翻译"：在约定的那一分钟到场，就是把尊重翻译成时间。不同文化对它的分量不同——有些文化把固定的钟点当作承诺，有些当作大致方向——这样的文化之间的误会古老而常见。但守时的算术在任何地方都一样：你的迟到，由每一个准时到场的人支付，一分一分地付，再乘以人数。一位迟到的演讲者面对两百人的大厅，从某种意义上说，花费了他人两百倍于自己的时间。守时还有一层私密的意义：习惯性迟到的人，通常会给自己讲一个动听的说法。准时是极少数不需要勇气、不需要金钱、也不需要天赋的道德行为——这恰恰解释了，为什么它的缺席能说明那么多事。
lessons.english: Punctuality is often treated as a small virtue, a matter of manners. In truth it is a form of translation: by arriving at the agreed minute, you translate respect into time. Cultures weigh this differently — some treat a fixed hour as a promise, others as a rough direction — and misunderstandings between such cultures are ancient and common. But the arithmetic of punctuality is the same everywhere: your lateness is paid for by everyone who arrived on time, minute by minute, multiplied by their number. A speaker who comes late to a hall of two hundred has spent, in a sense, two hundred times more of other people's time than his own. Punctuality also has a private meaning: those who are consistently late usually tell themselves a kind story about it. Being on time is one of the few moral acts that require no courage, no money and no talent — which is exactly why its absence says so much.

lessons.chinese: 旅行以"治愈偏见"闻名，但这个药方并不自动生效。一个游客可以环游世界，却只看见酒店、沙滩和一块屏幕。把旅行者与游客区分开的，是提问的质量。游客问："这里和家里比怎么样？"——答案永远是一份排名。旅行者问："这里为什么会是这样？"——答案永远是一个故事。旅行前最好的准备不是行李，而是谦逊：承认以不同方式生活的人，并不是"未完成版的我们"。每一种文化，都是针对真实难题——酷热、匮乏、历史——给出的漫长回答；还没弄懂问题就评判答案，是学不到东西的最快方式。所以，走得远，也要走得慢；行李少装一双袜子，也少装一点评判。旅行治愈偏见的名声，只对会提问的旅行者成立，而提问是头脑的习惯，不是双脚的习惯。换一个地方，只是换一扇窗外的风景。偏见会一直待在家里，除非你把它带出门，在开阔处检验。
lessons.english: Travel is famous for curing prejudice, but the cure is not automatic. A tourist can cross the world and see nothing but a hotel, a beach and a screen. What separates a traveller from a tourist is the quality of the questions asked. The tourist asks, "How does this compare with home?" — and the answer is always a ranking. The traveller asks, "Why is it like this here?" — and the answer is always a story. The best preparation for travel is not luggage but humility: the acceptance that people who live differently are not unfinished versions of ourselves. Every culture is a long answer to real problems — of heat, of scarcity, of history — and judging an answer before understanding its question is the fastest way to learn nothing. Travel widely, then, but travel slowly, and pack fewer judgements than socks. The famous cure of travel works only for travellers who ask questions, and questions are a habit of the mind, not of the feet. A change of place only changes the view outside the window. The prejudice stays at home until you carry it out and examine it in the open.

lessons.chinese: 屏幕与纸的竞赛没有决出赢家，而是形成了一种分工。屏幕赢得了存储、检索和夜间阅读；纸赢得了记忆、专注和睡眠。对比研究显示，读纸质书的读者记得所读内容的"形状"——某个想法在页面的哪个位置——而这种物理位置本身就是一种心理书签。屏幕邀请跳读，在页面间跳来跳去；纸则让眼睛和头脑减速，减到理解的速度。睡眠研究者还补充一条实用注脚：屏幕的光线会推迟纸质书自然带来的困意。但电子书有真实的优点——一手千卷，字体可调以照顾疲惫的眼睛，以及让远离书店的读者即刻拥有。聪明的读者两者都用，按目的选择：报纸与手册交给屏幕，值得朝夕相处的书交给纸。载体之间的竞争还会继续。阅读不该参与。
lessons.english: The contest between screens and paper ended not with a winner but with a division of labour. Screens won storage, search and night reading; paper won memory, focus and sleep. Studies comparing the two find that readers of paper remember the shape of what they read — where on the page an idea stood — and that physical position is itself a kind of bookmark for the mind. Screens invite skimming, popping between pages, while paper slows the eye and the mind to the speed of understanding. Sleep researchers add a practical note: the light of screens delays the drowsiness that books on paper bring naturally. Yet e-books carry real virtues — a thousand volumes in one hand, adjustable fonts for tired eyes, and instant access for readers far from any bookshop. The sensible reader uses both, choosing by purpose: screens for the newspaper and the handbook, paper for the book that deserves to be lived with. Formats will keep competing. Reading should not.

lessons.chinese: 独处与孤独是两种常常被世界混淆的状态。孤独是"缺少联结"的疼痛；独处是选择与自己共度时光，它是思想最古老的工具之一。作家、科学家与宗教的创立者都守护自己独处的钟点——不是因为他们不喜欢人，而是因为有些想法只在安静中开口。心理学家补充了一个现代警告：永不间断的连接让真正的独处变得稀有，而稀有的东西会变成一门需要练习的技艺。独处得好需要练习——一小时的没有屏幕、一次不带耳机的散步、一顿独自吃、不配视频的饭。练习者报告说有一种奇异的回报：他人意见的噪音被调低，自己的声音变得可闻。独处不是对社会的拒绝。它是一个人排练"如何成为一个人"的房间——以便当社会回来时，它遇见的是一个在家的人。学校、办公室和手机都默认我们应该随时被找到，而“随时可达”容不下那些绵长的思考。但深长的思考正是计划、书籍与心灵转变诞生的地方，它们需要一间自己的房间——在时间里，也在空间里。
lessons.english: Being alone and being lonely are different conditions that the world keeps confusing. Loneliness is the ache of missing connection; solitude is the choice to spend time with oneself, and it is one of the oldest tools of thought. Writers, scientists and founders of religions all guarded their hours alone, not because they disliked people, but because certain thoughts only speak in quiet. Psychologists add a modern warning: constant connection has made true solitude rare, and rare things become skills. To be alone well takes practice — an hour without a screen, a walk without headphones, a meal cooked for one without an accompanying video. Those who practise report a strange reward: the noise of other people's opinions turns down, and one's own voice becomes audible. Solitude is not a rejection of society. It is the room where a person rehearses being a person — so that when society returns, it meets someone at home. Schools, offices and phones all assume we should be reachable, and reachability leaves no room for the long thoughts. But long thoughts are where plans, books and changes of heart are born, and they need a room of one's own in time as well as in space.

lessons.chinese: 送礼看起来是一种朴素的善意，其实是人类所说的最复杂的语言之一。一份礼物同时说了三件事：我留意到你，我为你花了心思，我希望它适合你。这也解释了为什么钱——最灵活的礼物——常常最不能令人满足：它证明的是钱包，而不是关注。关于送礼的研究发现了一个规律性错误：送礼者追求惊艳与新奇，收礼者偏爱实用与用心。最好的礼物往往又小又具体：某人曾在闲谈中提过的一本书，一件能修好旧麻烦的工具。亲手做的礼物，每一块钱承载的情意最多，因为时间是没人能印制的货币。送礼还有一条分寸的义务：礼物不应把收礼者拖入人情债。完美的礼物，简而言之，是"注意力"的证明。它安静地说：在没有仪式要求的时候，你也在我心里。
lessons.english: Gift-giving looks like a simple kindness, but it is one of the most complicated languages humans speak. A gift says three things at once: I noticed you, I spent effort on you, and I hope this suits you. This is why money, the most flexible gift, is often the least satisfying: it proves the wallet, not the attention. Research on gift-giving finds a regular mistake — givers chase the impressive and novel, while receivers prefer the useful and thoughtful. The best gifts are often small and specific: a book someone mentioned once in passing, a tool that repairs an old annoyance. Handmade gifts carry the most meaning per yuan, since time is the one currency nobody can print. There is also a duty of tact: a gift should not trap the receiver into debt. The perfect gift, in short, is proof of attention. It says quietly: you were on my mind when no ceremony required it.

lessons.chinese: 习惯是一个已经睡着的决定。刷牙、系安全带、刷手机——这些都曾是选择，被反复演练到选择本身消失。习惯无善恶；它是引擎，方向取决于当初装进去的是什么。科学给出了一个简单的形成模型：一个信号、一个动作、一份奖励，重复到信号一响、动作自动开始。有用的发现是：信号与奖励可以保留，把中间的动作换掉——戒烟的人嚼口香糖，爱吃零食的人改喝茶。这就是为什么新习惯在"借用旧习惯的时间点"时最容易存活：晨啡之后立刻锻炼，上床之后立刻阅读。在故事里，功劳属于意志力；在生活里，干活的其实是重复。一次只改一个小回路，一年自然会照顾好它自己。这就是为什么新年决心总在二月失败：它们是没有回路的决定。把新的动作挂在旧的信号上——喝完茶就练习，穿上外套就散步——回路就会自己闭合。细小、无聊、不断重复——引擎和人生都是这样造出来的。
lessons.english: A habit is a decision that has gone to sleep. Brushing teeth, buckling a seatbelt, checking the phone — these were once choices, rehearsed until the choice disappeared. Habits are neither good nor evil; they are engines, and the direction depends on what was loaded into them. Science offers a simple model of how they form: a signal, an action and a reward, repeated until the signal alone starts the action. The useful discovery is that the signal and the reward can stay while the action in the middle is replaced — smokers chew gum, snackers drink tea. This is why new habits survive best when they borrow an old one's timing: exercise right after the morning coffee, reading right after climbing into bed. Willpower gets the credit in stories, but repetition does the work in life. Change one small loop at a time, and the year looks after itself. This is why New Year resolutions fail in February: they are decisions without a loop. Attach the new action to an old signal — tea, then practice; coat, then walk — and the loop begins to close by itself. Small, boring and repeated: that is how both engines and lives are built.

lessons.chinese: 看孩子玩耍，就是在看微缩的经济学、法学与工程学。一局弹珠游戏里有市场（弹珠易手）、有货币（好弹珠）、还有中央银行（拥有闪光弹珠的那个人）。把争执上诉给一个裁判，你就有了法庭；为一局新游戏发明规则，你就有了立法机构。孩子们还以少见的残酷和诚实做着"公平"实验：每个人都记得某个规则被专门为某个人发明出来的那一刻。人类学家在各大陆都找到了同样的游戏——捉迷藏、追逐、跳绳——因为童年的难题是全人类的：怎么藏、怎么追、怎么轮流。屏幕改变了布景，却没有改变本能：网络游戏依然靠团队、等级与轮替运转。有位哲学家说过，玩耍是儿童的工作。或许还可以补一句：它也是每个人人生中的第一届议会、第一个市场与第一所法学院。
lessons.english: Watch children at play and you watch economics, law and engineering in miniature. A game of marbles has a market (marbles change hands), a currency (the good marbles), and a central bank (whoever owns the shiny ones). Take a dispute to a judge, and you have a court; invent rules for a new game, and you have a legislature. Children also run experiments on fairness with unusual cruelty and honesty: everyone remembers the moment a rule was invented just for someone. Anthropologists find the same games on every continent — hide-and-seek, tag, jumping rope — because the problems of childhood are universal: how to hide, how to chase, how to take turns. Screens have changed the scenery but not the instincts: online games still run on teams, levels and turn-taking. Play, a philosopher once said, is the child's work. It might be added that it is the first parliament, the first market, and the first law school of every human being.

lessons.chinese: 这本书在英语对你开始的地方收尾：一份礼物。你拥有的每一个词都是被赠予的——由重复着音节直到你回应的父母，由订正你错误的老师，由电影、歌曲与街道上的陌生人。没有人"挣得"母语；母语是被接受的，而学习第二门语言，就是学习再一次接受。本书的六十篇课文，正是为了以同样的方式被接受而写：读中文，走向英文，对照，把你学到的留下。回译很慢，进步很安静，但它是真的——某一天，你会写出一个句子，然后发现语法自己想通了。那一刻，礼物完成了交接。语言不是一份要背的清单，而是一座要住进去的房子——由数百万使用者历经数百年建成；每位学习者都受欢迎，而且每位学习者终究会为它加建一个房间。欢迎入住。灯是亮的，功课已经开始了。
lessons.english: This book ends where English began for you: with a gift. Every word you own was given — by a parent repeating sounds until you answered, by a teacher correcting your errors, by strangers in films, songs and streets. Nobody earns a first language; it is received, and learning a second one is learning to receive again. The sixty passages in this book were written to be received the same way: read the Chinese, reach for the English, compare, and keep what you learn. Back-translation is slow, and progress is quiet, but it is real — one day you will write a sentence and find that the grammar thought of itself. That is the moment the gift changes hands. A language is not a list to memorise but a house to live in, built by millions of speakers over centuries; every learner is welcome, and every learner eventually adds a room. Welcome in. The light is on, and the study has already begun.

lessons.chinese: 祖父练了六十年的字，握笔的姿势从未变过。每天晚饭后，他在桌上铺开旧报纸，慢慢地研墨，一直写到灯芯烧低。他的字像他的人一样老实：端正、有点旧派、沉静而有力。我小时候替他研墨，他告诉我，笔要在手里立直，“像不肯弯腰的人”。他一辈子没卖过一幅字，尽管每年过年邻居都来求。给他们写门上的春联，他乐意；收钱，他从不碰。七十八岁那年他的手开始发抖，他把字写得更大，而不肯承认有什么变了。他去世后，我们在床底下找到四十年的习字，捆成捆，上面有他亲手写的日期。最后一张是临终前一周写的，笔画已弱，间架却依旧端正。我们都说，那字像他本人。
lessons.english: My grandfather practiced calligraphy for sixty years, and the way he held his brush never changed. Every evening after supper, he spread old newspaper across the table, ground the ink slowly, and wrote until the lamp burned low. His characters were honest the way he was honest: upright, a little old-fashioned, and quietly firm. As a boy I ground the ink for him, and he told me that the brush must stand upright in the hand, "like a man who refuses to bow." In all his life he never sold a single character, though the neighbors came asking every New Year. Couplets for their doors he wrote gladly; money he would not touch. When his hands began to tremble at seventy-eight, he wrote larger characters rather than admit that anything had changed. After he died, we found forty years of practice sheets under his bed, tied in bundles and dated in his own hand. The last sheet, written a week before the end, was weak in stroke but perfectly upright. It looked, we all agreed, like the man himself.

lessons.chinese: 四十年里，老全在村子和集镇之间摆渡，从未误过一个清晨。他的船旧却结实，船头用敲平的铁皮补过。他熟悉河的每一种脾气：八月哪里水流变懒，日出前哪里雾气最浓。三十年里船费一直是十分钱，谁要多给他都摆手不要。“河养活我，”他说，“河不讨价还价。”下雨天学生免费，清早新娘免费；他在座位下备了一袋干衣，给遭了暴雨的人。桥修起来以后，先是船没了，然后是乘客，最后再没有人可渡。听说他在空了的渡口坐了一个月，望着曾经有他船迹的水面。河还在那里，在我眼里比记忆里更宽，也不再需要他了。
lessons.english: For forty years old Quan rowed the river between our village and the market town, and in all that time he never missed a dawn. His boat was old but sturdy, patched at the bow with sheet iron hammered flat. He knew the river in each of its moods: where the current turned lazy in August, where the fog gathered thickest before sunrise. For thirty years the fare stayed at ten fen, and he waved away anyone who argued for more. "The river feeds me," he said, "and the river does not bargain." Schoolchildren crossed free in the rain; brides crossed free at dawn; he kept a sack of dry clothes under the seat for anyone caught in a storm. When the bridge was built, the boats went first, then the passengers, and at last there was no one left to carry. They say he sat on the empty slipway for a month, watching the water where his wake used to be. The river is still there, wider to my eyes now than memory allows, and no longer needing him.

lessons.chinese: 从我记事起，母亲的针线笸箩就放在炕角同一个位置。那是一只圆柳条筐，因年月而发黑，筐沿被磨得光滑，里面装着顶针、线、碎布，还有一把比我年纪还大的剪刀。她在夜里缝补，等灶间静下来，把灯拉近，让针脚接住灯光。只要一根线还没用尽，我们家的东西就不会被扔掉。袜子补到原来的毛线只剩记忆；床单翻面、缭边、再翻面。我的书包上打着三种颜色的补丁，每一块她都仔细挑过，“好让补丁看着像花，不像伤”。我曾为那些补丁难为情；如今我为它们骄傲。她老了、眼花以后，缝得少了，但笸箩从未离开那个墙角。她走后我们仍把它放在原处，到今天也没人敢去收拾它。
lessons.english: From as far back as I can remember, Mother's sewing basket sat in the same corner of the kang. It was a round willow basket, dark with age and worn smooth at the rim, holding thimbles, thread, scraps of cloth and a pair of scissors older than I was. She mended at night, after the stove went quiet, pulling the lamp close and letting the needle catch the light. Nothing in our house was thrown away while there was a thread left in it. Socks were darned until the original wool was only a memory; sheets were turned, hemmed and turned again. My school bag carried patches of three colors, each one chosen with care, "so the patch looks like a flower, not a wound." I was ashamed of those patches once; I am proud of them now. When she grew old and her eyes failed, she sewed less, but the basket never left its corner. After she was gone we kept it where it stood, and to this day no one has dared to tidy it.

lessons.chinese: 邮局后面、骑楼底下，有一位修表匠，他听不见，也不会说。大家都叫他老姚，这一带的人都有一块被他打开过至少一次的表。人们说，他什么也听不见，却听得见表：把它贴在耳边，闭上眼睛，从滴答声里读出它的毛病。他的铺子是一间斗室，一盏灯、一枚放大镜和一把椅子，那椅子修过的次数比送来的表还多。顾客把毛病写在纸条上，他读纸条像别人听人说话，又快又没有不耐烦。然后他点点头，交谈便到此为止。经他修过的表回来调整，一律不收费，无论多旧。有一次一位游客为赶时间要多给钱，他用一根手指把钞票推了回去。他退休以后，骑楼下的卷帘门关了许多年，好像那铺子只是睡着了。人们至今记得他两只手做过的两件事：点头，和那只说着“等一等”的、平平摊开的手掌。
lessons.english: Behind the post office, in the arcade, worked a watchmaker who could not hear and did not speak. Everyone called him Yao, and everyone in the district carried a watch he had opened at least once. He heard nothing, people said, yet he could hear a watch: hold it to his ear, close his eyes, and read its trouble in the tick. His shop was a cupboard of a room — one lamp, one loupe and a chair mended more often than the watches brought in. Customers wrote their complaints on slips of paper, and he read them the way other men listen, quickly, without impatience. Then he nodded, and that was the whole conversation. A watch he had repaired came back for adjustment free of charge, however old. Once a tourist offered extra for hurrying, and he pushed the notes back across the counter with one finger. When he retired, his shutter stayed down for years, as if the shop were only sleeping. People still remember the two things he did with his hands: the nod, and the flat palm that said wait.

lessons.title_en: The Storyteller of the Old Teahouse
lessons.chinese: 每天下午两点，说书人登上老茶馆的三级台阶，在桌上拍一下，满屋便静了。白先生说的是老书：三国的将、水浒的好汉、公案里的判官。他从不用书，却能凭记忆背出四十回，而且同一个故事从来不说两遍一个样。打仗他用手指敲出鼓点；伤心处他把嗓子沉成一缕线。每一回总在最险处收住，只留一句：“要想知道后事如何，明天再来。”满座叹一声气，笑一阵，再添一壶茶。他的报酬是豁了口的碗里收的铜板，他都分给门口的瞎眼琴师。收音机来了，接着电视来了，茶馆一年比一年空。最后一个下午，他把一部四十年从未说完的书说完了一回。然后他朝空着的长凳一排一排作揖，走下那三级台阶。
lessons.english: Every afternoon at two, the storyteller climbed the three steps of the old teahouse, rapped the table once, and the room fell silent. Master Bai told the old cycles: generals of the Three Kingdoms, heroes of the marsh, judges of the court tales. He never used a book, yet could recite forty chapters from memory, and never told a tale the same way twice. Battle scenes he gave in drummed fingers on the table; sorrow he gave in a voice that sank to a thread. A chapter always ended at the moment of greatest danger, with one sentence: "If you want to know what happens next, come back tomorrow." The audience groaned, laughed, and ordered more tea. He was paid in coppers from a chipped bowl, and shared them with the blind fiddler by the door. Radio came, then television, and the teahouse emptied year by year. On the last afternoon he finished, for once in forty years, a tale he had never finished. Then he bowed to the empty benches, row by row, and came down the three steps.

lessons.chinese: 二十六年里，石桥街的邮差是个叫申屠的人，整条街拿他对表。他的车铃隔着两个院子就能听见，总是响两遍：一遍在街角，一遍在你家门前。他送信、送包裹、送汇款单，冬天清晨还送来哪位邻居病了的第一条消息。凡不属于他的信他一字不看，四十年里没人撞见他看过一封开口的信封。送不到的信他收在抽屉里，每个月再试一次，直到找到地址，或者找到人。有一封这样的信他送了九年才送到，那家人在信前流泪时，他就站在门口等。他退休时，全街为他摆了一桌送行的席面，家家端来一个菜。他只讲了几句话，末了说：“我只送过属于你们的东西，其余的路是路自己走完的。”如今的信由一辆白色小面包车中午送到，从不迟到；但街坊们还在念叨那声铃响两遍的声音。
lessons.english: For twenty-six years the postman of Stonebridge Street was a man called Shentu, and the street set its clock by him. His bicycle bell could be heard two courtyards away, always rung twice: once at the corner, once before your gate. He delivered letters, parcels and money orders and, on winter mornings, the first news of which neighbor was ill. He read nothing that was not his to read, and in forty years no one caught him looking at an open envelope. Undeliverable letters he kept in a drawer and tried again every month, until the address was found or the person was. One such letter took him nine years to deliver, and he stood at the gate while the family wept over it. When he retired, the street gave him a farewell banquet, and every household brought one dish. His speech was short, and ended: "I only carried what was yours; the road did the rest." Mail now arrives in a small white van at noon, never late; but the neighbors still speak of the sound of a bell rung twice.

lessons.chinese: 方圆二十里只有方医生一家诊所，三十八年里他的自行车认得乡里每一条小路。他在省城读的书，本可以留在那里；他回来了，用他的话说：“总得有一个知道你奶奶叫什么的医生。”他的诊室就是他的厨房，药香和饭香混在一起。他用小学生作业本记账，一半的页脚都是同一个字：欠。孩子们吃药配有糖；害怕的人听他讲笑话治病。他曾踩着一夜的大雪去接一个难产，事后还谢绝了答谢的酒席。镇医院带着新设备开张，病人离开了他；新设备让他们犯难时，他们又回来了。他收费始终按老价钱，只涨过一次，据他说，是因为物价。诊所如今是一间杂货铺，可老病人路过门口，仍像在跟老朋友的家打招呼。
lessons.english: Doctor Fang kept the only clinic for twenty li around, and for thirty-eight years his bicycle knew every path in the district. He was educated in the provincial capital and could have stayed there; he came back because, as he put it, "someone has to be the doctor who knows your grandmother's name." His consulting room was also his kitchen, and the smell of herbs mixed with that of rice. He kept accounts in a school exercise book, and half the pages ended with the word, owed. Children took their medicine with sugar; the frightened were treated with jokes. He once walked all night through snow to reach a difficult birth, and refused the thank-you feast afterwards. When the township hospital opened with new equipment, the patients left him; when the new equipment puzzled them, they came back. He charged the old rate to the end, raising it once, he said, on account of prices. The clinic is a grocery store now, but old patients still greet the doorway the way one greets an old friend's house.

lessons.title_en: The Barber under the Locust Tree
lessons.chinese: 市场东头的老槐树下坐着剃头匠金师傅，身边是他全部的家当：一条凳、一只炉、一盆水，和一条磨剃刀的荡刀布。这手艺是父亲传给他的，而父亲又是从县里走乡串镇的剃头挑子那里学来的。四十年里他涨过三次价，每次都提前两周带着歉意通知。老人们来是为了刮脸多于理发：热毛巾、慢刀子，还有那些问你儿子、问你膝盖的闲话。他备着一面缺了一角的镜子，摆放的角度让裂纹落在你脸的外面。开学第一天给孩子剃头不收钱，好让运气跟他们走进新教室。对街开了带电推子的理发店，他看着，不发一言；五年之内那些店都关了，条凳还在树下。他说，最后一批客人来坐的成分和来刮脸的一样多。他去世时那棵槐树比我们都老，如今也比关于他的记忆更老。
lessons.english: Under the big locust tree at the market's east end sat the barber Jin with his whole establishment: a stool, a stove, a basin and a razor strop. His father taught him the trade, as his father had learned it from the traveling barbers of the county town. His prices rose three times in forty years, each rise announced with an apology two weeks ahead. Old men came for the shave more than the haircut: the hot towel, the slow blade, the talk that asked after your son and your knee. He kept a mirror broken at one corner and turned it so the crack fell outside your face. Children were cut free on the first day of school, so luck would travel with them into the new classroom. When barbershops with clippers opened across the street, he watched without comment; within five years they were gone, and the stool stayed under the tree. His last customers, he said, came as much to sit as be shaved. When he died the tree was older than any of us, and older now than the memory of him.

lessons.chinese: 父亲的脸，我记得不如他的手清楚。那是瓦匠的手，手掌宽厚，左手拇指上有一道凿子打滑留下的疤。那双手砌过给我们取暖的灶台，院墙裂过两次、砌过两次，也砌过我出生的那座房子的每一块砖。吃饭时它们显得对筷子来说太大，动作里带着一种近乎温柔的仔细。表达满意，他用手而不是用话：肩上重重一拍，对我的意义超过任何夸奖。他最后一年，那双手安静地放在毯子上，我第一次注意到指节已经像老树根一样鼓起。我握住其中一只，它回握的力量，和当年把我从河里提起来时一样。临终前他对我说，砖石活会旧；手记得的，它就一直记得。如今我的手也是同样的宽掌，当我发觉自己在用目光丈量一面墙时，我知道这是谁的习惯留了下来。
lessons.english: I cannot picture my father's face as clearly as I can picture his hands. They were a mason's hands, wide at the palm, with a scar across the left thumb where a chisel had slipped. Those hands built the hearth that warmed us, raised the courtyard wall twice when it cracked, and laid every brick of the house I was born in. At dinner they looked too large for the chopsticks, and moved with a carefulness that was almost tender. Approval he expressed with them, not with words: a heavy pat on the shoulder that meant more than any praise. In his last year, when they lay quiet on the blanket, I noticed for the first time how the knuckles had swollen like old tree roots. I held one of them, and it held back with the same grip that had once lifted me out of a river. Masonry fades, he told me near the end; what a hand remembers, it remembers. Mine now carry the same broad palm, and when I catch myself measuring a wall with a glance, I know whose habit has outlived him.

lessons.title_en: The Man Who Collected Old Things
lessons.chinese: 每十天，收旧货的就沿我们的巷子来一趟，扁担横在肩上，吆喝的声音像一支被抽走了调子的歌。他收铜、收铅、收书、收骨头，也收一切带着记忆的东西。孩子们把牙膏皮卖给他，为的是挤净最后一口牙膏；母亲们卖给他被老鼠咬破的衬衫。他给价很少，还价更少，收去的东西都转卖，只是从没人知道卖给了谁。有一回他几乎分文不取地回绝了一对明式椅子，说它们应当去一个肯让它们体面变老的人家。一捆东西，他掂掂捆它的绳子就能报出内容。饥荒年月，他把米悄悄留给那些把能卖的都卖给了他的人家。废品站取代他以后，他看着新来的板车，仍在阴凉里喊他的指点。“看钉子，”他对年轻收货人说，“钉子比木头更会告诉你一件东西的年纪。”是他第一个教我懂得，物件也记账，而且有些要用敬意来还。
lessons.english: Every ten days the junk man came down our alley, pole across his shoulder, calling in a voice like a song with the tune taken out. He bought copper, lead, books and bones, and anything with a memory attached to it. Children sold him toothpaste tubes for the last squeeze of paste; mothers sold him shirts chewed by mice. He paid little and haggled less, and what he bought he resold, though nobody ever learned to whom. Once he declined a pair of Ming-style chairs for almost nothing, saying they should go to someone who would let them grow older with respect. He could name the contents of a bundle by weighing its string. In the lean years he quietly left rice with families that had sold him everything sellable. When the scrap station replaced him, he watched the new carts and still called advice from the shade. "Look at the nails," he told the young collectors; "nails tell the age of a thing better than wood." He was the first to teach me that objects keep accounts, and that some are owed respect.

lessons.chinese: 流过我们村的那条溪，在源头只有一掌宽，你踮脚就能跨过去，连鞋跟都不会湿。春天先到那里，比山下的村子早一周，有时早十天。最早的迹象是一种气味而不是一种颜色：湿土、冷石，还有一丝没有名字的甜。然后是沿岸的毛茛，年成好时密得让溪水像在黄色里流淌。鸟按固定的次序回来，像捏着票：鹡鸰先到，燕子随后，布谷要等开犁才来。老婆婆们说，布谷是把种子喊进土里的，从没有人证明她们说错。到五月，溪水深得能让男孩用当天破的竹篾编的篮子罩小鱼。后来我在名胜之地见过许多春天，花更好，桥也更好；没有一个比源头那个来得更早。如果春天有一座都城，我的都城就是那一掌宽的水。
lessons.english: The stream that runs past our village is only a hand wide at its source, and you can step across it without wetting your heel. Spring arrives there first, a week or ten days before it reaches the houses below. The first sign is a smell rather than a color: wet earth, cold stone and something faintly sweet that has no name. Then come the buttercups along the banks, so thick in a good year that the water seems to run yellow. The birds return in a fixed order, as if they held tickets: the wagtail first, the swallow next, the cuckoo only when the plowing starts. The old women say the cuckoo calls the seed into the ground, and no one has ever proved them wrong. By May the stream is deep enough for boys to trap minnows in baskets woven from bamboo split that morning. I have seen springs in famous places since, with better flowers and better bridges; none of them arrived earlier than the one at the source. If spring has a capital, mine is that hand-wide water.

lessons.title_en: Summer Nights on the Threshing Floor
lessons.chinese: 七月里，麦子进了仓，打谷场就成了村里的大堂屋。天光暗下去，各家搬出竹床和粗席，占下自己的一方地面，像圈定地盘。石面把白天的热存得很久，没有人在意；夜里的气味是铡碎的麦秸、蚊烟，还有谁家的西瓜。老人们谈收成和价钱；妇人们谈亲事；孩子们本该睡觉，却在数星星。殷奶奶的鬼故事讲得太好，讲到一半，全场的人都会朝火堆挪近一点。有时远处铁路上有火车经过，那声音穿过田野而来，像从别国过来的天气。我们一直睡到露水下来，母亲们抱着被子出现，用日食般的权威结束这个夜晚。打谷场如今是水泥的了，麦子由机器烘干；再没有人在那里睡，星星也失去了观众。可是七月的夜里，我在城里的床上翻身，仍在听那列远处的火车。
lessons.english: In July, after the wheat was in, the threshing floor became the village's common room. As the light failed, families carried out bamboo beds and coarse mats and claimed their squares of ground like territories. The stone held the day's heat a long time, and nobody minded; the night smelled of cut straw, mosquito smoke and someone's watermelon. The old men talked harvest and prices; the women talked marriages; the children were supposed to sleep and counted stars instead. Grandmother Yin told ghost stories so well that halfway through, the whole floor would shift a little closer to the fire. Sometimes a train passed on the far line, and its sound came across the fields like weather from another country. We slept out until the dew came, when mothers appeared with quilts and ended the evening with the authority of an eclipse. The floor is concrete now, and the wheat is dried in machines; no one sleeps there, and the stars have lost their audience. But on July nights I still turn over in my city bed and listen for the far train.

lessons.chinese: 翻越西岭的小道要爬两个小时，不属于任何个人，也许正因如此，它被一双双脚养得很好。秋天一到，它就成了一份文书：每一场风都在上面留下一行字。先是松针，细而匀，像给这个季节画下的尺子线；随后是阔叶，栎和枫，镶出铜色和血色的边。板栗啪的一声落下来，滚到路边，持长竿的男孩们像债主一样在那里等着。山上的空气有了棱角，干净得像在冷水里洗过的刀。从垭口望下去能看见三个县，一个比一个安静，炊烟在凝滞的空气里立得笔直。下山快，落叶在脚下碎开，像一阵放慢的掌声。山下什么地方，一条狗对一个生人吠了两声，想想又觉得不必，重新趴下。这页文书山只保存一个月，至多六周；随后冬雨把字迹溶掉，小道重新只是小道。
lessons.english: The path over West Ridge takes two hours to climb and belongs to nobody in particular, which is perhaps why it is so well kept by feet. In autumn it becomes a document: every wind leaves a line of writing on it. The pine needles come first, fine and even, like a rule drawn for the season; then the broad leaves, oak and maple, in margins of copper and blood. Chestnuts fall with a click and roll to the edge, where boys with long sticks await them like creditors. The air up there has an edge to it, clean as a blade washed in cold water. From the saddle you can see three counties, each quieter than the last, chimney smoke standing straight in the still air. Going down is faster, and the leaves give way underfoot with a sound like slow applause. Somewhere below, a dog barks twice at a stranger, thinks better of it, and lies down again. The mountain keeps this page a month, six weeks at most; then winter rain dissolves the writing, and the path goes back to being only a path.

lessons.chinese: 我十二岁那年冬天的一个黄昏，雪开始下，轻柔、认真，没有风。等广播报出积雪的数字时，它已经漫过窗台，把整条巷子的狗都弄哑了。我们把小桌挪近炉子，母亲把火烧得很足，像她在那些要紧的夜晚所做的那样。父亲朗读报纸，跳过政治那版；母亲剥花生，剥进一只碗，那碗慢得让人不敢相信。窗外的世界正在被修改：篱笆胖了，车辙平了，喧闹的街道变得又短又白。水壶整晚低声说话，没有人忍心叫它停。我记得自己那时想：雪是在替天空做家务，而我们都是它的客人。这样的夜晚无法计划，只能认出；这就是它们的全部艺术。四十年过去，只要黄昏下雪，我仍会把一把椅子挪得比那个夜晚所需要的离火更近。
lessons.english: Snow began at dusk one evening in my twelfth winter, soft, businesslike, without wind. By the time the radio said how much had fallen, it had already climbed past the windowsill and silenced the dogs of the whole lane. We pulled the small table close to the stove, and my mother made the fire generous, the way she did on nights that mattered. Father read the newspaper aloud, skipping the politics, and mother shelled peanuts into a bowl that emptied too slowly to be believed. Outside, the world was being edited: hedges fattened, ruts smoothed, the loud street made brief and white. The kettle spoke in a low voice all evening, and no one had the heart to ask it to stop. I remember thinking that the snow was doing housework for the sky, and that we were its guests. Such nights cannot be planned, only recognized; that is their whole art. Forty years on, whenever snow falls at dusk, I still set a chair closer to the fire than the night requires.

lessons.chinese: 江南的雨不是一件事，而是一种心境的气候。它与其说在落，不如说在沉降，细得像筛过的面粉，耐心得像知道债稳的债主。雨里，白墙变成旧象牙的颜色，河道由玉色变成石板色。在那里，伞是装饰；真正的本地人光着头走，让雨来决定他们本来要走多远。声音的传播很奇怪：巷尾一支橹的声音，会先于自己屋顶上的雨声进入你的耳朵。这样的雨里，老城照旧赴它的约：茶馆九点坐满，学校四点放学，桥上照例聚着一伙不像渔民的渔民。年轻人抱怨潮湿和霉斑，这不算冤枉；可他们的祖辈说起梅雨，用的是对一位难处亲戚的温柔。是雨写出了这座城，而这座城已经学会在雨里读自己。我在更坏的天空下住过，那里的阳光更多而天气更少；如今我知道自己是被哪一种造就的。
lessons.english: The rain of Jiangnan is not an event but a climate of mind. It does not so much fall as settle, fine as sifted flour, patient as a creditor who knows the debt is good. Under it the white walls go the color of old ivory, and the canals turn from jade to slate. Umbrellas there are ornaments; the true natives walk bareheaded, letting the rain decide how far they had meant to go. Sounds carry strangely: an oar at the end of the lane reaches your ear before the rain drumming on your own roof. In such rain the old town keeps its appointments: the teahouse fills at nine, school lets out at four, and the bridge collects its usual unconvincing fishermen. Younger people complain of damp and mildew, which is fair; but their grandparents speak of the plum rains with the tenderness owed to a difficult relative. The rain wrote the town, and the town has learned to read itself in it. I have lived under harsher skies that gave more sunshine and less weather; I know now which formed me.

lessons.title_en: The Bridges of the Small Town
lessons.chinese: 故乡在步行二十分钟的半径里有十一座桥，并为哪一座最老而愉快地争吵。其中四座是石拱桥，桥顶被九百年的脚步磨出一层浅浅的润光。有两座纯粹是功能，又平又混凝土，全城都不肯爱它们。其余几座介于两者之间，像我们大多数人一样。每座桥都带着自己的行当：南桥清早是鱼，庙桥脚下是剪刀，而钱桥上有一个给婴儿称重的人。桥理好了全城的感情：求婚在旧灯桥的桥心举行，每扇窗都看得见进展如何。洪水来了又去，桥拱以行家的平静承受它们。最后带走其中两座的不是水，是进步；如今城里人说起那些旧渡口，像截肢者说起一条不见了的肢体里的天气。我梦见那些桥的次数，多过梦见桥之间的街道；这告诉我，我的童年砌在什么上面。
lessons.english: My hometown kept eleven bridges within a radius you could walk in twenty minutes, and quarreled happily about which was the oldest. Four of them were stone arches, worn at the crown into a shallow gloss by nine hundred years of footsteps. Two were pure function, flat and concrete, and the town refused to love them. The rest were somewhere in between, like most of us. Each bridge had its trade: fish at South Bridge at dawn, scissors at the foot of Temple Bridge, and at Money Bridge a man who weighed babies. The bridges ordered the town's feelings: courtships were held mid-span on Old Lamp Bridge, and every window had a view of how they went. Floods came and went, and the arches took them with the calm of professionals. In the end it was not water but progress that carried two of them away, and the town still speaks of the old crossings like amputees speaking of weather in a missing limb. I dream of those bridges more often than of the streets between them, which tells me what my childhood was built on.

lessons.chinese: 我记得最清楚的一场雾，是六月里一个下午四点从海上进港的，来时不打招呼。前一刻海港还是一幅画；下一刻它成了关于自己的传闻。视野变小的时候，声音变大：缆索在唱，什么地方一台水泵在咳，码头上每一声脚步都带上了戏剧腔。平日无人看一眼的灯塔，成了世上唯一确凿的事实。老渔夫在原地坐下，像庄稼人在晌午那样，用把潮汐当历法的耐心等着。近处一个男孩朝白色里喊一个名字，先是着急，后来是为了好玩，听那名字变了个样子回来。雾是海的提醒：它想去陆地做客，随处都行。一小时后雾散，那些船像被一只淘气的手重新摆过，人人去查自己的缆绳，神气像离家多年刚回来的人。太阳回来时只是一枚谦逊的圆盘，海港重新摆好画面，对自己的信心少了一分。
lessons.english: The fog I remember best came in from the sea at four in the afternoon, in June, without calling ahead. One moment the harbor was a picture; the next it was a rumor of itself. Sound grew larger as sight grew smaller: rigging sang, a pump coughed somewhere, and every footstep on the pier became theatrical. The lighthouse, which nobody looks at in clear weather, became the only fact in the world. Old fishermen sat down where they stood, the way farmers do at noon, and waited with the patience of men whose calendars are tides. A boy nearby kept calling a name into the whiteness, first anxiously, then for the pleasure of hearing it come back changed. Fog is the sea's reminder that it may visit the land wherever it likes. When it lifted an hour later, the boats seemed rearranged by a mischievous hand, and everyone checked their moorings like people back after years away. The sun returned as a modest disk, and the harbor resumed its picture, one degree less certain of itself.

lessons.chinese: 通往我大学的慢夜车要走十一个小时，如今同样路程只要九十分钟，但我不愿交换。它逢站必停，那些停靠就是全部的演出。每个小站，灯光像舞台一样落在站台上：一个提灯的站务员，两个讲故事的搬运工，一条受过教育、懂得等待的狗。半夜，小贩们沿车窗走过，托着厚玻璃杯的茶，提着篮子里的鸡。站与站之间，乡野放映它无声的胶片：一户亮灯的农舍，一行白杨，道口信号的闪烁，然后又是黑暗。陌生人分享梨子和各自的生平，到早晨，他们对彼此村庄的了解超过了自己的家人。我什么也没记，却什么都记得，就像你记得一张脸，而记不住一段文字。如今快车趁茶还烫就把路赶完，这很有效率，也不留下任何可记的东西，这算一种偷窃。有时我仍特意去坐慢车，避开旺季，那些小站为三名观众亮起灯来。
lessons.english: The slow night train to my university took eleven hours for a journey that now takes ninety minutes, and I would not trade. It stopped everywhere, and the stops were the entertainment. At each small station, light fell on the platform like a stage: a guard with a lamp, two porters telling a story, a dog educated enough to wait. Vendors moved along the windows at midnight with tea in heavy glasses and chickens in baskets. Between stations the country offered its silent reels: a lit farmhouse, a line of poplars, the wink of a crossing signal, the dark again. Strangers shared pears and biographies, and by morning knew each other's villages better than their own families did. I wrote nothing down and remembered everything, the way you remember a face and not a paragraph. The express now covers the distance while the tea is still hot, which is efficient, and leaves nothing to remember, which is a kind of theft. Sometimes I take the slow train anyway, out of season, and the stations light up for an audience of three.

lessons.chinese: 出了城里最后一排房子，公路认输、缩成一条小径的地方，芦苇开始了，一直铺到天边。那不是风景，是一个国家，有自己的边界、季节和水的政治。秋天一到，全国同时转成银色，风穿行而过，声音像大海在排练。我们撑一条平底小船走窄水道，桨使不上力的地方就用篙。芦苇在船后合拢得那样彻底，十米就像隔着一辈子的距离。白鹭单腿立着，专心致志；水鼠横过船尾的航迹，像赶着上班的职员那样匆忙。芦苇每年冬天割去编席、苫顶，一到春天，这个国家又重建了自己，颜色更浅，满怀希望。如今那里是湿地公园，铺着塑料木板步道；说句公道话，白鹭的观众比它们想要的多。可是那种声音需要迷路作代价，如今迷路已经不被允许。
lessons.english: Beyond the last houses of the town, where the road gave up and became a footpath, the reeds began and ran on to the horizon. They were not scenery but a nation, with its own borders, seasons and a politics of water. In autumn the whole country turned silver at once, and the wind passing through it made a sound like the sea rehearsing. We took the narrow channels in a flat-bottomed skiff, poling where the oar was useless. The reeds closed behind the boat so completely that ten meters felt like distance from another life. Egrets stood on one leg, absorbed; water rats crossed our wake with the briskness of clerks late for office. Every winter the reeds were cut for mats and roofing, and by spring the nation had rebuilt itself, paler and hopeful. Today the marsh is a wetland park with a walkway of plastic planking, and the egrets, to be fair, have more visitors than they ever wanted. But the old sound requires getting lost, and that is no longer permitted.

lessons.chinese: 我们连夜爬山，一共十二个人，被彼此的呵欠和抱怨拴在一起。山间客栈说过，云层很低，天亮时我们将站在石头上，脚下就是天空。四点半，世界是一块黑布和一口口白气，信念所剩不多。然后，没有任何仪式，东方泛出桃子皮的颜色，云的海底亮起来，像灯上蒙的纸。太阳升上来时不是一个球，而是一片平平的金色海洋，在动，我们的影子长长地蓝蓝地躺在上面，比山本身还高。整整一分钟没有人说话；连节俭的向导也忘了他的口头禅。我们中间的一位教师毫无难为情地哭了，解释说：“这个内容我用挂图教了二十年。”太阳升起十分钟后，山下的村庄才醒进白昼；我们看着他们迟到地继承一个我们已经过完的早晨。下山路上遇见往上爬的人；他们问值不值，我们答得太快，听着反而不诚实。
lessons.english: We climbed through the night, twelve of us, roped to one another's yawns and complaints. The inn had said the clouds were low, and that at dawn we would stand on stone with the sky beneath our feet. At half past four the world was black cloth and cold breath, and faith was running low. Then, without any ceremony, the east turned the color of a peach skin, and the floor of cloud lit from below like paper over a lamp. The sun rose not as a ball but as a level gold sea, moving, our shadow lying on it long and blue, taller than the mountain. For a full minute nobody spoke; even the thrifty guide forgot his sayings. A schoolteacher among us wept without embarrassment, and explained, "I have taught this for twenty years from diagrams." The sun was up ten minutes before the village below woke into daylight, and we watched them inherit, late, a morning we had finished. On the way down we met them climbing; they asked whether it was worth it, and we said yes too quickly to sound honest.

lessons.chinese: 我记忆里随身的那本词典，不是如今书架上的这本，而是一本厚厚的红皮书，书脊松了。它是我十四岁那年县作文比赛的奖品；为坐车回家，父亲用牛皮纸把它包了起来。六年里它跟着我的帆布包走，吃进墨水、油渍，和我坐过的每一张课桌的气味。那时查过的词，至今仍翻得开它们的页：书自己摊在“命运”一词上，在“舍弃”一词上，在那条意思是“一切”的长词条上。读者的词典就这样变成一部自传。有一个词的页边，我最好的朋友用铅笔写过一个错的译法，我一直没有改；他不在了，那条错的注释也就留着。买了新的词典，齐全，也新，看上去像一间雇来的屋子：里面没有一样东西记得我。我在那里查词，得到答案，此外学不到什么。旧的那本我收在抽屉底层；有些晚上我读页边，我的青春在那里作着注。
lessons.english: The dictionary I carry in my memory is not the one on my shelf now, but a fat red one with a loose spine. It was my prize from the county composition contest of my fourteenth year; for the bus ride home, my father had it wrapped in kraft paper. For six years it traveled in my canvas bag, taking in ink, oil and the smell of every desk I sat at. Words I looked up then still open to their pages: the book falls open of itself at the word fate, at abandon, at the long entry that means everything. A reader's dictionary becomes an autobiography in that way. Beside one word my best friend had penciled a wrong translation, and I never corrected it; he is gone, and the gloss stays. When I bought the new dictionary, complete and up to date, it looked like a hired room: nothing in it remembered me. I look things up there, get my answer, and learn nothing else. The old one I keep in the bottom drawer; some evenings I read the margins, where my youth is annotated.

lessons.title_en: The First Time I Left Home
lessons.chinese: 第一次离家我十七岁，去省城的路要坐一段慢船、一段慢车，花掉大半天。母亲在外衣夹层里缝了四十块钱，告诉了我第三区我们亲戚的住处。我带着煮鸡蛋、一包苏打饼干，和一封用我们生产队最庄重的字写的介绍信。船上有柴油和橘子的气味；河面宽得有自己的天气。每到一处码头，都有看上去像天下顶要紧人物的人下船，船每空一次，我就胆大一分。进了城，嘈杂是从皮肤进来的：公共汽车、喇叭，还有塔楼上带着威风报时的大钟。我找到学校，签了名，在台阶上吃了一个鸡蛋，不知道那就是幸福。那天夜里我写平生第一封家信，写了四句，第五句因为反复看地址没有写成。多年后我才知道，母亲把那封信收在她的纸盒里，连信封一起，直到纸沿着折痕断开。
lessons.english: The first time I left home I was seventeen, and the journey to the provincial capital took a slow boat, a slow bus and most of a day. My mother had sewn forty yuan into the lining of my jacket, and told me where our relative lived in the third district. I carried boiled eggs, a bag of soda crackers and a letter of introduction in our team's most formal hand. The boat smelled of diesel and oranges; the river was wide enough to have weather of its own. At every landing someone got off who looked like the most important traveler alive, and the boat felt emptier and braver each time. In the city the noise entered through the skin: buses, loudspeakers, and a tower clock striking with authority. I found the school, signed my name, and ate one egg on the steps, not knowing it was happiness. That night I wrote my first letter home in four sentences, and could not write the fifth for checking the address. Years later I learned that my mother kept that letter in her box of papers, envelope and all, until it broke along its folds.

lessons.title_en: The Swallows of the Old House
lessons.chinese: 每年春天，一对燕子回到堂屋的梁上，日子由它们自己定，不与任何人商量。它们在旧巢原处重修，一间一间地加盖，好像房子可以无限地改善下去。祖母不许我们碰那根梁，并在巢下放了一只旧篮子，接住落下来的东西。燕子，她说，只肯在年内不出岔子的人家做窝，她说这话时像在陈述定案。于是我们在它们底下小心地过日子：喂雏的时辰把饭桌上的话放低，从四月到九月，门用一块石头撑着。小燕子面朝屋子等着，一张张张开的嘴像五个小小的问句。它们终于飞起来的时候，全家人不知怎么都觉得被引见了一次。老屋拆掉的那年，燕子按时来到，绕着废墟打转；那天晚饭谁都没有说话。盖新房的人向我们担保，新房子可以设计得把它们挡在外面，也确实如此。从那以后我再没有住过有燕巢的屋檐下，而且我觉察到了这一点。
lessons.english: Every spring, on a date the swallows decided without asking anyone, a pair returned to the beam over our main room. They rebuilt last year's nest where it stood, adding on room by room, as if a house could be improved indefinitely. My grandmother forbade us to touch the beam, and put an old basket under the nest to catch what fell. The swallow, she said, only nests over a household that will not go wrong during the year, and she said it as settled fact. So we lived under them carefully: dinner conversation lowered at feeding time, the door propped open with a stone from April to September. The young birds faced the room and waited, their mouths open like five small questions. When the young ones finally flew, the whole family somehow felt introduced. The year the old house was torn down, the swallows arrived on time and circled the rubble; nobody spoke at dinner that evening. The builders assured us that new houses could be designed to keep them out, and were. I have not lived under a swallow's nest since, and I notice.

lessons.title_en: The Fever of My Seventh Year
lessons.chinese: 我七岁那年冬天，在后屋躺了三个星期，一场烧让墙纸都呼吸起来。医生每隔三天来一趟，自行车靠在门框上，冷却时发出嗒嗒的响声。他话很少，按我的腕，看我的眼睛，每次只说同样的两个字：还烧。母亲坐在床边做那些可以边做边守的活计，好让屋子听不见她的害怕。声音穿过高烧进来，尺寸全不对：磨盘的轱辘声从很远的地方来，一只勺子放在桌上，响得像钟。父亲夜里踩着雪去药铺，把药揣在大衣里带回来，暖得像一块出炉的面包。烧退的那天早上，邻居家的牛犊落地；确切年份我记不确，就是这样给它定的位。原来虚弱自有它的一方国土，去窗前一趟再回来，就算一次远征。母亲哭过一回，在厨房里，放着水声；墙纸继续呼吸，轻了些，像被安抚下去了。
lessons.english: The winter I was seven, I lay for three weeks in the back room with a fever that made the wallpaper breathe. The doctor came every third day on a bicycle that ticked as it cooled against the door frame. He spoke little, pressed my wrist, looked at my eyes, and said the same two words each visit: still burning. My mother sat by the bed doing mendable work, so that the house would not hear her fear. Sound arrived through the fever in the wrong sizes: the grinding of the millstone came from very far away, and a spoon set down on the table rang like a bell. My father walked to the pharmacy through the snow at night and brought the medicine back inside his coat, warm as a loaf. The fever broke on the morning the neighbors' new calf was born; the exact year escapes me, and that is how I date it. Weakness, it turned out, is its own country, with journeys to the window and back counted as expeditions. My mother cried once, in the kitchen, with the water running; the wallpaper breathed on, quieter, like something dismissed.

lessons.chinese: 就我所能看见的，外婆一共有三件布衫，蓝的那件是出门穿的。那是靛青色，染得深得发潮，钉着五粒像小耳朵一样的布纽扣。蓝衫去赶集，去吃喜酒，去看医生；有一次折在牛皮纸里，去了两百里外我母亲的家，作为一份被谢绝又悄悄退回的礼物。她自己洗它，一个人，在星期一洗，晾在里屋的绳上，免得客人看见它滴水。平日她穿灰的那件；蓝衫像候场的戏子一样等着。她去世时，蓝衫在前屋，刷过、扣好、放平，朝着她不会再用的那扇门。我母亲最先摘下了纽扣，像人们从要倒的房屋里先救下那扇门。如今有一粒在我这里，收在抽屉里一些不值钱的东西中间；我发现，真的东西都往这种地方聚。布会褪色，寻常的染料会认输，靛青撑得住；手掌还记得五只小耳朵。
lessons.english: My grandmother owned, as far as I could see, exactly three blouses, and the blue one was for going out. It was indigo, dyed so deep it looked wet, with five cloth buttons shaped like small ears. The blouse went to market, to weddings, to the doctor, and once, folded in brown paper, to my mother's house two hundred li away, as a gift refused and quietly returned. She washed it herself, alone, on Mondays, and hung it on the inside line where visitors would not see it dripping. On workdays she wore the gray one; the blue one waited like an actress in the wings. When she died, the blue one was in the front room, brushed, buttoned, laid flat, facing the door she would not use again. My mother took the buttons off before anything else, the way people save doors from a falling house. I have one of them now, in a drawer with things of no value, which is where, I find, the true things collect. Cloth fades; ordinary dyes give up; indigo holds; the hand keeps its memory of five small ears.

lessons.title_en: The Washing Stones by the River
lessons.chinese: 村子把新闻放在河边，放在一级级被磨成浅浪的石阶上。天亮之前直到晌午，妇人们垫着卷席跪在那里，把一个村子洗进水里。棒槌的起落是村子的第二只钟，每个女人都靠它读时辰。跪在下游最末一位的人最先听见一切：亲事、口角、价钱，还有谁家儿子从城里来了信。我母亲用换洗的次序换消息，像大臣们换粮食那样。石阶是一个有自己的座次的议会；被派来取衣服的我，官职最小：传送那些棒槌的节奏装不下的口信。冷天里，妇人们的手变成水的颜色，指节发红，没有人提起，因为年年都提起。我小学最后一年，村里来了洗衣机，石阶从下头开始长苔。新闻搬到了店铺门口，后来又搬进手机；石阶还在那里，托着浅浪，等着水来读。
lessons.english: The village kept its news at the riverside, on a flight of stone steps worn into shallow waves. From before light until noon, the women knelt there on rolled mats, washing the town into the water. The beat of the beater was the village's second clock, and every woman read the day by it. Whoever knelt lowest downstream heard everything first: engagements, quarrels, prices, and whose son had written from the city. My mother traded washing turns for news the way statesmen trade grain. The stones were a parliament with its own seating order, and I, sent to fetch the washing, held the lowest office: runner of messages too long for the beater's rhythm. In the cold months the women's hands went the color of the water, red at the knuckles, and nobody mentioned it, because it was mentioned every year. A washing machine came to the village in my last year of primary school, and the steps grew moss from the bottom up. The news moved to the shop front and then to the phones, but the stones are still there, holding their shallow waves, ready for the water to read.

lessons.chinese: 那只猫走了，就我们所能判断的，是出于原则，在他九岁那年的十月。他灰色，白胸脯，吃饭讲究时刻，不轻易受用别人的亲热，除非按他自己的日历。我们沿巷子四个角落喊了他一个星期；妹妹画了一张像，供销社的墙上替我们贴了一个月。头场雪之后，我们用过去式说他，声音放轻，像掩上一扇已经扣不上的门。他四月回来，瘦了，一只耳朵底下带着一道逗号似的疤，走进厨房，像办完一件短差事回来。他不道歉，也不解释；他喝了水，睡了十八个钟头，重新开始他对这个家的管理。我父亲什么都不承认，那个星期却被人看见把好鱼摆了出去。他去过哪里，我们始终没有弄清；那道疤就是他交回的全部报告。他又活了四年，隔壁两回盖房子他都照睡不误，最后一次离开，和他头一次一样，没有仪式，也是在十月。
lessons.english: The cat left, as far as we could tell, out of principle, in the October of his ninth year. He was gray with a white chest, methodical about meals, and unbothered by affection except on his own calendar. We called for him at the four corners of the lane for a week; my sister made a drawing, and the cooperative store pinned it up for a month. By the first snow we spoke of him in the past tense, quietly, the way one closes a gate that no longer latches. He returned in April, thinner, with a scar like a comma under one ear, and walked into the kitchen as if returning from a short errand. He did not apologize and did not explain; he drank, slept eighteen hours, and resumed his administration of the household. My father, who admits nothing, was seen that week putting out the good fish. Where he had been we never learned; the scar was the whole of his report. He lived four more years, slept through two houses being built next door, and left for good as he had left, without ceremony, in October.

lessons.chinese: 放映员蹬着板车到村，幕布的消息比他跑得还快。孩子们吃过中饭就用砖头占前排，一块砖一个座，整个下午守着边界。幕布挂在两棵白杨之间，它的两面都有观众，一面看电影，一面看看电影的人。发电机咳了几声，稳下来，整片黑暗一齐向前倾。有些片子我们熟得能背，比演员快半秒念出台词，放映员装作没听见。风把幕布吹得晃动时，人脸上的波纹像隔着水看东西；孩子们一致认为，这反而更好。第三本片子放到哪里，母亲的手摸到我的头，停在那里；我一动不动，像守着一只落在身上的鸟。黑地里走回家是电影的下半场：灯笼在几条小路上排开，关于情节的争论跨着水沟继续。后来我知道，有墙的电影院更暖、更干燥、更舒服；可从没有人说它更好。
lessons.english: The projectionist arrived by pedaled cart, and the news of the screen traveled faster than he did. Children claimed the front with bricks before lunch, one brick one seat, and defended the border all afternoon. The sheet went up between two poplars, and both sides of it had an audience, one watching the film and one watching the watchers. The generator coughed, steadied, and the whole darkness leaned forward at once. We knew some films by heart and recited the lines a half-second ahead of the actors, which the projectionist pretended not to hear. When wind shook the sheet, faces rippled like things seen through water, and that, the children agreed, improved everything. Somewhere in the third reel my mother's hand found my head and rested there; I kept very still, the way one does with a bird. The walk home in the dark was part of the film: lanterns strung out along the paths, plot arguments continuing over the ditches. A cinema with walls, I later learned, is warmer, drier and more comfortable; no one has ever claimed it was better.

lessons.chinese: 停电停在一个平常的星期二晚饭时，巷口的变压器拖出一声低长的音，像一条船在下决心。我们点饼干盒里存的蜡烛头吃饭，那盒子专为这样的场合而存，也就是说，为高兴而存。父亲被黑暗禁了报纸，改讲一个故事，很长，分章节，按蜡烛烧的速度现编。妹妹发现她手的影子可以教会狗叫。收音机没了用处，站在架子上像一位退役的运动员，也没有人嫌它。谈话不知从哪一刻起不再是填充，成了正题：祖父战乱年月的一张轮船票，对折着，在他的钱包里躺了五十年。灯十点半回来，突然而且粗鲁，大家都缩了一下，像白天没有敲门就闯进屋子。父亲合上他没有打开的报纸，说今天电来得早。我们把蜡烛一支一支慢慢吹灭，像放一根缆绳，让黑暗把夜晚收完。
lessons.english: The power failed at supper on an ordinary Tuesday, and the transformer at the lane's mouth let out a long low note, like a ship deciding. We ate by candle stubs kept in a biscuit tin for occasions like this one, which is to say, for pleasure. My father, forbidden by darkness from his newspaper, told a story instead, a long one, with chapters, invented at the pace of the candle. My sister found that the shadow of her hand on the wall could be taught to bark. The radio, useless, stood on the shelf like a retired athlete, and nobody minded it. At some point the conversation stopped being a fill-in and became the thing itself: grandfather's steamer ticket from a war year, half folded, fifty years in his wallet. The lights returned at half past ten, sudden and rude, and everybody flinched, as if day had broken into the room without knocking. Father closed the newspaper he had not opened and said the electricity was early. We blew out the candles slowly, one by one, the way you pay out a rope, and let the dark finish the evening.

lessons.title_en: The White Shirt of Graduation Day
lessons.chinese: 毕业那天全校穿白衬衫，我那件是头天晚上洗的，在洗衣石上拧干，又压在粮箱底下。县里来的照相师把我们排在台阶上，像解析一个句子，从高到矮，教师坐在当中。校长讲前途；蝉讲炎热；前途和炎热都赢了。同桌三年的他站在我旁边；九月里我们约好，到最后要说点什么。我们什么也没说；有人说，底片等不得。照片里我的领子笔挺，脸瘦，眼睛已经望向往后十年我要给他写信的那个人。那年秋天他南下进了工厂；我进了山里的师范；信写了四年，交情写到第五十年。他署名还用我们旧的教室编号，好像房间能留住人。那一天我记得一件照片装不下的东西：那件衬衫压在粮箱底下的、确切的重量。
lessons.english: On graduation day the whole school wore white shirts, and mine had been washed the night before, wrung out on the washing stone, and pressed under the grain box. The photographer came from the county, and we were arranged on the steps like a sentence being parsed, tallest to shortest, teachers seated in the middle. The headmaster spoke about the future; the cicadas spoke about the heat; the future and the heat both won. My deskmate of three years stood beside me, and we had promised, in September, to say something at the end. We said nothing; the film, someone said, could not wait. In the photograph my collar is perfect, my face thin, my eyes already looking toward the person I would write to for ten years. He went south that autumn to a factory; I went to teachers' school in the hills; the letters lasted four years and the friendship has lasted fifty. He signs himself with the old classroom number, as if rooms could keep people. Of that day I remember one thing the photograph does not hold: the exact weight of that shirt under the grain box.

lessons.chinese: 如今一切慢的东西都受怀疑，好像它必定藏着什么，因为诚实的东西不会要这么久。我们造出了在我们问完之前就作答的机器，并且学会了把停顿当成冒犯。可是我看重的每一种本事，都是用手的速度、而不是用线的速度学会的。读书慢，懂得更慢，而性子是最慢的。竹子在地下待四年、再用六个星期长成，自有一番道理；它的耐心不是生长的中断，而是生长的形状。慢不是倒退；走得慢的人，仍可以第一个到达别人只是绕着打转的目的地。我们所说的效率，常常只是看得见的那一半的快，而看不见的那一半，账单在后头。不妨一试：工工整整写一个字，不碰手机走完一条街，从第一个音符听到最后一个音符。慢不是做事的方法；慢是一样东西变成你的东西所需要的速度。
lessons.english: Everything slow is under suspicion now, as if it must be hiding something, since nothing honest takes so long. We have built machines that answer before we finish the question, and we have learned to feel the pause as an insult. Yet every skill I value was acquired at the speed of the hand, not the speed of the wire. Reading is slow, understanding is slower, and character is the slowest of all. The bamboo that takes four years underground and six weeks to rise is a proverb for a reason; its patience is not a pause in growth but the shape of it. Slow does not mean backward; a slow walker can still be the first to arrive at a destination that others only circle. What we call efficiency is often just the quickness of the visible half, with the invisible half billed later. Try this: write one character with care, walk one street without the phone, listen to one song from the first note to the last. Slowness is not a method for doing things; it is the speed at which things become yours.

lessons.chinese: 我们学校后面有一块方方的草地，一个学期之内，草地中央出现了一条路。没有人规划它；它是一个一个想省十二步的人，一步决定一寸地定下来的。草先沿着对角线认输，随后土认输，小路成了事实，规划的人只好在下一张图上把它画进去。那条小路我想了许多年，因为它是我见过的最清楚的一课：路究竟是怎样发生的。路是结论，不是前提。欲望在有人画线之前，早就走过那块地方许多遍；画线只是承认走路的那一刻。风俗、集市和名声也是一样：它们是被重复踏出来的小径，然后才围起来、起名字。当然，捷径也会错；我们那条六月里过水，最后围了起来，而那时已经投过两代人的票。每一张地图都是先前行走的档案，每一个行人都是无名的测量员，不计酬，也不问许可。
lessons.english: Behind our school there was a square of grass, and across it, over one term, a path appeared. No one laid it out; it was decided, foot by foot, by people who wanted to save twelve steps. The grass gave up first along the diagonal, then the soil gave up, and the path became a fact that the planners had to include on the next map. I have thought about that path for years, because it remains the clearest lesson I have ever seen in how roads actually happen, as against how they are announced. Roads are conclusions, not premises. Desires walk across a place long before anyone draws the line, and the drawing is only the moment the walking is admitted. The same is true of customs, markets and reputations: they are paths worn by repetition, then fenced and named. Of course a shortcut can be wrong; ours flooded in June and was finally fenced off, and by then two generations had voted. Every map is an archive of earlier walking, and every walker is an unnamed surveyor, working without pay or permission.

lessons.chinese: 我的书房有一盏灯，在这单独的一盏灯下，屋里住着两群居民：东西，和它们的影子。光亮得着称赞，影子得着怜悯，可是这笔安排比这更有意思，也更古老。灯不只照出书桌；它把椅子举成一个长臂的巨人，让挂钩上的外套长出另一只肩膀。每一盏强光都在墙上创造自己的民间传说。人也是这样：站在光里的，投出的形状比本身大，而且形状先到。这不是不公道；这是光学，名声不过是带了日期和人名的光学。老画师们懂得这笔账：他们只给人物一盏灯，让影子扛起画面的其余部分，画面反而更大了。熄了灯，两群居民溶进黑暗这一种人人平等里，那里没有什么高于自己，也没有什么低于自己。这时我懂了为什么思想偏爱夜晚，为什么那么多智慧从吹灯开始。
lessons.english: My study has one lamp, and by its single light the room keeps two populations: the things, and their shadows. Brightness gets the praise and shadow gets the pity, but the arrangement is more interesting, and older, than that. The lamp does not only reveal the desk; it raises the chair into a long-armed giant and lets the coat on the hook grow another shoulder. Every strong light creates its own folklore on the walls. People are like that too: what stands in the light casts a shape larger than itself, and the shape arrives first. This is not unfairness; it is optics, and reputation is simply optics with dates and names. The old painters understood the economy: they gave the figure one lamp and let the shadow carry the rest of the picture, and the picture got larger. When I turn the lamp off, the two populations dissolve into one democracy of the dark, where nothing is more than itself and nothing is less. Then I understand why thinking prefers the evening, and why so much wisdom begins by putting out the light.

lessons.chinese: 等待名声不好，好像它是时间的口袋，值钱的东西都被摸走了。但进门先要分清：有一种等待把等的人掏空，有一种等待把等的人养熟。柜台前的长队掏空人；炉边的面团养熟人；久未回音的长信，要么养熟，要么放馊，要看写信的人，看信里敢存什么指望。我们怨恨等待，怨的不是时长，而是无助，是自己成了一件搁在架子上的包裹，由别人的计划写地址。解药不是快，而是把包裹变成园丁：在等待里种一点什么，等待就成了一个季节。我做过的每一个成熟的决定，都是在我当时全心怨恨的一段等待之后做出的。不耐烦凑近了看，通常是戴着秒表的害怕。老话说这个词是“养熟”，这个词同样用果子、用委屈、也用人。等，不是因为事情会自己变好，而是因为你会；事情停在原处，你却在加深。
lessons.english: Waiting has a bad reputation, as if it were time's pocket, picked clean of everything valuable. But a distinction must be made at the door: there is waiting that empties the waiter, and waiting that ripens him. The queue at the counter empties; the dough by the stove ripens; the long letter unanswered ripens or sours, depending on the writer, on what the letter dares to hope. What we resent in waiting is not duration but helplessness, the sensation of being a parcel on a shelf, addressed by other people's plans. The cure is not speed; it is conversion of the parcel into the gardener: plant something in the waiting, and the waiting becomes a season. Every mature decision I have ever made was made after a waiting that I resented with my whole heart at the time. Impatience, examined closely, is usually fear wearing a stopwatch. The old word for it was ripening, and the word applied equally to fruit, to grievances and to persons. Wait, not because the thing will improve by itself, but because you will; the thing stays put, and you deepen.

lessons.chinese: 我们悄悄接受了破即完结，这个决定显现在我们的房间里，也显现在我们的关系里。从前，裂了的碗要打孔、上锔钉，锔钉是黄铜的，碗带着一枚勋章回去干活。锔钉不装作瓷器；那是一道诚实的缝，每位客人都看得见，客人们把它读成履历。修补假定时间是真实的：东西会延续，延续值得出力气，而一段损伤的历史并不是历史的终点。更换恰好相反，它假定器物只是它的功能，而这一课会从抽屉漏进心里。人如今也是被更换，而不是被修补，有时下手的是人自己。可是人和碗一样，也是它遭遇了什么的那份记录，而一份毫无瑕疵的记录，通常是一份短的记录。那么，能修的就修，并且让补痕露着：缝里嵌金也好，黄铜也好，素线也好，哪一样说真话就用哪一样。要点从来不是把裂纹藏起来；要点是碗比裂纹活得长。
lessons.english: We have quietly accepted that broken means finished, and the decision shows in our rooms and in our relations. A cracked bowl used to be drilled and stapled, the staples were of brass, and the bowl went back to work with a medal. The staple did not pretend to be porcelain; it was an honest seam, visible to every guest, and the guests read it as biography. Mending assumes that time is real: that things continue, that continuance is worth labor, and that a history of damage is not the end of a history. Replacement assumes the opposite, that the object is only its function, and the lesson leaks from the drawer into the heart. People, too, are now replaced rather than mended, sometimes by their own hands. But a person, like a bowl, is also the record of what happened to it, and a flawless record is usually a short one. Mend what you can, then, and let the mend show: gold in the seam, or brass, or plain thread, whichever tells the truth. The point was never to hide the crack; the point is that the bowl outlives it.

lessons.chinese: 安静不是无声；把这两者混为一谈，我们付出了屋子里最好的几间房。无声是一种缺席，被强制的或仅仅是偶然的，而且让人发痒。安静是一种在场，是修来的，是各种声音之间保持距离的协议。你在洒扫时辰的庙里听见过它，在运笔的画室里，在汤刚刚开口说话的那一刻的厨房里。安静自有结构：一个声音被接纳，占住讲台，其余一切便不必再表演。噪音不是响；噪音是许多声音个个要求成为唯一，这也正是我们对一场争吵的定义。修习安静曾经是日子里的固定内容：收音机关掉之后的那一个钟头，没有目的的散步，没有谁催促的一顿饭。我们把那些钟头一间一间拆掉，然后奇怪自己的思想去了哪里，倒好像搬走的不是房客自己。无论失去什么，留一间安静的房；那是屋里唯一一间，思想肯脱鞋进来的房。
lessons.english: Quiet is not silence; the confusion between them costs us the best rooms in the house. Silence is an absence, enforced or merely accidental, and it itches. Quiet is a presence, achieved, an agreement among sounds to keep their distance. You hear it in a temple at the hour of sweeping, in a studio under the brush, in a kitchen at the moment the soup begins to speak. Quiet has a structure: one sound, accepted, holds the floor and releases everything else from performing. Noise is not loudness; noise is many sounds each demanding to be the one, which is also our definition of a quarrel. The practice of quiet used to be built into days: the hour after the radio went off, the walk without a destination, the meal nobody hurried. We demolished those hours one by one, then wondered where our thinking went, as if the tenant were not the one who had moved out. Keep one quiet room, whatever else you lose; it is the only room in the house where the mind takes off its shoes.

lessons.chinese: 水是我们所知最温柔的东西，也是搬得动巨石的那一个。它的方法里没有戏剧：坚持，一个水平面，以及乐于随容器改变形状而并不把容器的形状错当成自己的。洪水是水有一季忘了礼数；运河是水接受了雇佣；清晨窗上的露，是水在有礼貌地登门。人们劝人学水，而通常以为那只是指退让。可是退让只是脾气的一半：另一半是水平，是地面不平就绝不肯安歇的那份坚持。水不同石头争辩；它天天照面，一次课也不缺，直到石头成了卵石，争论结束。它用同一只手托船、也掀船，没有人说它反复无常；我们只说天气坏。那么，学完整的脾气吧：软到能取任何形状，平到对公道存着记忆，耐到等得过花岗岩。那不是温柔；那是不需要吵嚷的力气。
lessons.english: Water is the gentlest substance we know and the one that moves the boulders. Its method has no drama in it: persistence, a level, and a willingness to take the shape of the container without confusing it with its own. Floods are water forgetting its manners for a season; canals are water accepting employment; the dew on the window at dawn is water calling on you politely. People are advised to be like water and usually imagine that it means yielding only. But yield is half the temper: the other half is levelness, the standing refusal to rest while the ground is uneven. Water does not argue with the rock; it attends, daily, without missing a session, until the rock is a pebble and the argument is over. It carries boats and capsizes them with the same hand, and nobody calls it inconsistent; we call the weather bad. Learn the whole temper, then: soft enough to take any shape, level enough to keep a memory of fairness, patient enough to outwait granite. That is not gentleness; it is strength that has no need of noise.

lessons.chinese: 纪念碑都修给记忆，可日常的苦力多半是忘却在做。要想起一张脸，另外五十张必须退下；要在人群里听清一个词，一千个词必须被打发走。忘却不是丢失，而是把单据烧掉的挑选。心智留下用得着的，把其余的付之一炬；我们看不见那场火，是一种慈悲。疼痛大声地教相反的一课，坚持什么都别放走；可是疼痛只要给足年头，也会替我们忘。悲伤过后留下的不是伤口，而是伤口压进我们的形状，就像压花留住花，留不住那个季节。怨恨是忘却的失职；教训是它的尽职；同一件事两者都能当，看它归进哪只抽屉。我见过什么都记得、什么都不饶恕的人，他们驮着自己的过去，像骡子驮货，有效率，而没有体面。有福的记忆有一个称职的门房，知道什么时候把门关上，什么时候轻轻放人群回家。
lessons.english: Memory gets the monuments, but forgetting does most of the daily labor. To recall one face, fifty others must stand down; to hear one word in a crowd, a thousand must be dismissed. Forgetting is not loss but selection with the paperwork destroyed. The mind keeps what it can use and burns the rest, and it is a mercy that we do not watch the fire. Pain teaches the opposite lesson loudly, insisting that nothing be let go; but pain, given years, also forgets on our behalf. What remains after grief is not the wound but the shape it pressed into us, the way a pressed flower keeps the flower and not the season. A grudge is forgetting's failure; a lesson is its success; the same event can be either, depending on the drawer it is filed in. I have known people who remembered everything and forgave nothing, and they carried their pasts the way mules carry loads, efficiently and without honor. Blessed is the memory with a good doorman, who knows when to hold the door and when, gently, to let the crowd go home.

lessons.chinese: 种一棵树，是为一个你多半不会出席的将来投的一票。坑是为一个尚不存在的人挖的；树荫许给陌生人，许给未生的孩子，许给还没选定的狗。没有别的一样寻常举动，把慷慨和耐性混得这么彻底；这就是为什么各村的纠纷都信任老树作证。树作证得很慢，它的证据是一圈圈的年轮。谚语说，种树最好的时间是二十年前，其次是现在；谚语说得对，而且说得厚道，谚语很少这样冒险。果树用更短的地平线教同一课：今年开花，夏天忍耐，最后是甜；而且不许拔起来看根。我们改种更快的：篱笆、意见、名声；然后纳闷自己的树荫怎么这样薄。挖坑要挖得比根要求的更宽，浇水要浇过第一场绿；你眼前这棵树，不是将来那棵树。今年种一点什么吧，种一样在你只剩家谱上一道笔划时还站得住的东西。
lessons.english: Planting a tree is a vote for a future you will mostly not attend. The hole is dug for a person who does not exist yet; the shade is promised to strangers, to children not born, to dogs not chosen. No other common act mixes generosity and patience so completely, which is why old trees are trusted witnesses in every village dispute. A tree argues slowly, and its evidence is rings. The proverb says the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago and the second best is now; it is right, and kind, which proverbs seldom risk. Fruit trees teach the same lesson with a shorter horizon: blossom this year, patience through the summer, sweetness at last, and no pulling up to check the roots. We plant faster things instead, hedges, opinions, reputations, and then wonder that our shade is thin. Dig the hole wider than the roots ask, and water past the first green; the tree you see is not the tree there will be. Plant something this year that will be standing when your name is only a stroke on a family page.

lessons.chinese: 年老被当作一个没人打算去访问的国家的天气来报道，而人人都在去那里。报道两头都不准：它既不是年轻人想象的那种废墟，也不是老年人广告里的那种安慰。它实际上是一次换币：力气花得早，见识攒得晚。老人输掉身体的争论，只要留心，就赢得对格局的争论：这个笑话他们从前见过，如今看得见它往哪里去。年轻是一笔漂亮的借入；年老，运气好的话，是所有权。羞辱是真的：那个躲在舌尖上的词，那段从前不算什么的楼梯。但另一面有工资：事物终于各是各的分量，而大多数事物，原来几乎没有分量。艺术不在于跟日历作战，而在于兑换：把够得着换成深，把快换成准，把喝彩换成留意。听说对一生的最后一次盘点很短，能留下来的那句话，不是他做成了什么，而是他是个什么样的人。
lessons.english: Age is reported like weather from a country nobody means to visit, and everyone is going there. The reports are wrong both ways: it is neither the ruin the young imagine nor the consolation the old advertise. What it actually is, is a change of currency: strength is spent early, and what accumulates late is seeing. The old lose the argument of the body and win, if they attend, the argument of the pattern: they have seen the joke before, and now see where it is going. Youth is a beautiful loan; age, with luck, is ownership. The humiliations are real: the word hiding on the tip of the tongue, the stair that used to be nothing. But there is a wage on the other side: things finally weigh what they weigh, and most things, it turns out, weigh little. The art is not to fight the calendar but to convert: trade reach for depth, speed for aim, applause for attention. The last review of a life, I am told, is short, and the sentence that survives is not what he achieved but what he was like.
